question.text: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F} = \langle z, \,0, \, 2 \rangle$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as \[ \displaystyle \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \,\bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}} \: \textrm{d}A. \] Which of the following could be the missing expression?
question.explanation:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

  • the upper surface $S_1: z = g(x,y) = 1 - \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ is oriented upward, and

  • the lower surface $S_2: z = h(x,y) = 0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

  • Consider the upper cone $S_1.$

    We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(1 - \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\right) = -\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(1 - \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\right) = -\dfrac{y}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

    If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then \[ P = z = 1 - \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}, \qquad Q = 0, \qquad R = 2. \]

    As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have \begin{align*} \iint\limits_{S_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} & = \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D -\left(1 - \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\right) \cdot \left(-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}}\right) - 0 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{y}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}}\right) + 2 \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} - x + 2 \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

  • Consider the lower plane $S_2.$

    Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n} = \langle 0,0,-1 \rangle.$ As a result, we have \begin{align*} \iint\limits_{S_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} & = \iint\limits_{S_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}S \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D \langle z, 0, 2 \rangle \cdot \langle 0, 0, -1 \rangle \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D -2 \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across the entire surface is \begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} & = \iint\limits_{S_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} + \iint\limits_{S_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} - x + 2 \: \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_D -2 \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{ \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} - x} \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F} = \langle z^2, \, 0, \, y \rangle$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as \[ \displaystyle \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \,\bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}} \: \textrm{d}A. \] Which of the following could be the missing expression?
question.explanation:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

  • the upper surface $S_1: z = g(x,y) = \sqrt{4 - x^2 - y^2}$ is oriented upward, and

  • the lower surface $S_2: z = h(x,y) = 0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

  • Consider the upper hemisphere $S_1.$

    We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\sqrt{4 - x^2 - y^2}\right) = -\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{4 - x^2 - y^2}} \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{4 - x^2 - y^2}\right) = -\dfrac{y}{\sqrt{4 - x^2 - y^2}} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

    If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then \[ P = z^2 = 4 - x^2 - y^2, \qquad Q = 0, \qquad R = y. \]

    As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have \begin{align*} \iint\limits_{S_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} & = \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D - (4 - x^2 - y^2) \cdot \left(-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{4 - x^2 - y^2}}\right) - 0 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{y}{\sqrt{4 - x^2 - y^2}}\right) + y \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D x\sqrt{4 - x^2 - y^2} + y \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

  • Consider the lower plane $S_2.$

    Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n} = \langle 0,0,-1 \rangle.$ As a result, we have \begin{align*} \iint\limits_{S_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} & = \iint\limits_{S_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}S \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D \langle z^2, 0, y \rangle \cdot \langle 0, 0, -1 \rangle \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D -y \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across the entire surface is \begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} & = \iint\limits_{S_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} + \iint\limits_{S_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D x\sqrt{4 - x^2 - y^2} + y \: \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_D -y \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{ x\sqrt{4 - x^2 - y^2} } \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F} = \langle 0, \, -z, \, 2y \rangle$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the cone $z=4-\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and the plane $z=0.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as \[ \displaystyle \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \,\bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}} \: \textrm{d}A. \] Which of the following could be the missing expression?
question.explanation:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

  • the upper surface $S_1: z=g(x,y)=4-\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is oriented upward, and

  • the lower surface $S_2: z=h(x,y)=0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

  • Consider the upper cone $S_1.$

    We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(4-\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\right) = -\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(4-\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\right) = -\dfrac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

    If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then \[ P = 0, \qquad Q =-z= \sqrt{x^2+y^2}- 4, \qquad R = 2y. \]

    As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have \begin{align*} \iint\limits_{S_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \Big( -(0) \cdot \left(-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \right) - \Big(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}-4\Big) \cdot \left(-\dfrac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \right) + 2y\Big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \left(y - \dfrac{4y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}+2y\right) \: \textrm{d}A\\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \left(3y - \dfrac{4y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\right) \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

  • Consider lower plane $S_2.$

    Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}=\langle 0,0,-1 \rangle.$ As a result, we have \begin{align*} \iint\limits_{S_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_{S_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}S \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \langle 0,-z,2y \rangle \cdot \langle 0,0,-1 \rangle \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D (-2y) \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_{S_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} + \iint\limits_{S_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \left(3y - \dfrac{4y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\right) \: \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_D (-2y) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{y - \dfrac{4y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}} \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F} = \langle -y, \, 0, \, x \rangle$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the hemisphere $z=1-\sqrt{9-x^2-y^2}$ and the plane $z=1.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as \[ \displaystyle \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \,\bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}} \: \textrm{d}A. \] Which of the following could be the missing expression?
question.explanation:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

  • the upper surface $S_1: z=g(x,y)=1$ is oriented upward, and

  • the lower surface $S_2: z=h(x,y)=1-\sqrt{9-x^2-y^2}$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

  • Consider the upper plane $S_1.$

    Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}=\langle 0,0,1 \rangle.$ As a result, we have \begin{align*} \iint\limits_{S_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_{S_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}S \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \langle -y,0,x \rangle \cdot \langle 0,0,1 \rangle \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D x \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

  • Consider lower hemisphere $S_2.$

    We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y){:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\Big(1-\sqrt{9-x^2-y^2}\Big) = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{9-x^2-y^2}} \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\Big(1-\sqrt{9-x^2-y^2}\Big) = \dfrac{y}{\sqrt{9-x^2-y^2}} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

    If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then \[ P = -y, \qquad Q =0, \qquad R = x. \]

    As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have \begin{align*} \iint\limits_{S_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= -\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= -\iint\limits_D \left( -(-y) \cdot \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{9-x^2-y^2}} - (0) \cdot \dfrac{y}{\sqrt{9-x^2-y^2}} + x \right) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= -\iint\limits_D \left(\dfrac{xy}{\sqrt{9-x^2- y^2}} +x \right) \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_{S_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} + \iint\limits_{S_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D x \: \textrm{d}A - \iint\limits_D \left(\dfrac{xy}{\sqrt{9-x^2- y^2}} +x \right) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D x-\dfrac{xy}{\sqrt{9-x^2- y^2}} -x \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{-\dfrac{xy}{\sqrt{9-x^2- y^2}}} \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F} = \langle 0, \, x, \,y \rangle$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the hemisphere $z=\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}$ and the plane $z=1-\dfrac{1}{2}x.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as \[ \displaystyle \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \,\bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}} \: \textrm{d}A. \] Which of the following could be the missing expression?
question.explanation:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

  • the upper surface $S_1: z=g(x,y)=\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}$ is oriented upward, and

  • the lower surface $S_2: z=h(x,y)=1-\dfrac{1}{2}x$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

  • Consider the upper hemisphere $S_1.$

    We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}\right) = -\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}} \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}\right) = -\dfrac{y}{\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

    If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then \[ P = 0, \qquad Q =x, \qquad R = y. \]

    As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have \begin{align*} \iint\limits_{S_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \Big( -0 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}}\right) - x \cdot \left(-\dfrac{y}{\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}}\right) + y \Big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \left(\dfrac{xy}{\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}} + y\right) \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

  • Consider lower plane $S_2.$

    We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y){:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(1-\dfrac{1}{2}x\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2} \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(1-\dfrac{1}{2}x\right) = 0 \\[5pt] \end{align*}

    If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then \[ P = 0, \qquad Q =x, \qquad R = y. \]

    As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have \begin{align*} \iint\limits_{S_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= -\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &=- \iint\limits_D \Big( -0 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) - x \cdot 0 + y \Big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &=- \iint\limits_D y \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_{S_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} + \iint\limits_{S_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \left(\dfrac{xy}{\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}} + y\right) \: \textrm{d}A - \iint\limits_D y \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\dfrac{xy}{\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}} } \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}
